issues.legal_issue: Land held by members of a landowning family must be included in calculating permissible area, subject to the separate-unit treatment for adult sons and the aggregate limit on the family and those units.
material_facts: The landowner’s wife and sons held land in their own names, and the dispute concerned whether their holdings could be excluded when determining the family’s permissible area.
On the appointed day, the family included one adult son and three minor sons.
The revenue authorities treated the family and the adult son as entitled to two units, while the High Court directed that the permissible area be determined separately for the individual petitioners.
issues.conclusion: The High Court erred in treating the wife’s separately held land as giving her an independent permissible area and in excluding family members’ holdings from the calculation. A member’s land must be taken into account with the family’s land; an adult son is treated as a separate unit, but the family’s land and the separate units’ land together cannot exceed the aggregate limit.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 3(e) and 3(n) define family and person; Section 4(1) sets the permissible area for a family, Section 4(4) treats every adult son as a separate unit subject to an aggregate limit, and Section 4(6) requires the land held by a person who is a family member to be considered together with the land held by the family members. Section 6 imposes the ceiling on land held by a person. The Court held that the plain language of Section 4 did not support treating a wife’s separately held land as outside the family calculation.

predicates.land_ceiling_determination: The proceeding determines the permissible area under a land-ceiling regime.
predicates.family_member_holds_land: A person who is a member of a landowning family holds land.
predicates.adult_son_holds_land: An adult son of a landowner holds land.

issues.definition: When a land-ceiling determination concerns land held by a family member or an adult son, the family and separate-unit holdings are included in the calculation subject to the aggregate ceiling.

issues.legal_issue: The principle of stare decisis does not prevent correction of an earlier interpretation when the governing statutory text is clear and the earlier decision postdates the proceedings in which it is invoked.
material_facts: The respondents relied on an earlier Full Bench decision to support the High Court’s interpretation.
The Court found the relevant statutory provisions clear rather than ambiguous.
The proceedings had begun before the Full Bench decision was delivered.
issues.conclusion: Stare decisis did not prevent the Court from rejecting the earlier interpretation and setting aside the High Court’s judgment.
issues.legal_principle: Relying on Gajnan v. Seth Brindaban and Raj Narain Pandey v. Sant Prasad Tewari, the Court stated that stare decisis may support a long-standing interpretation where statutory meaning is ambiguous and admits more than one interpretation. Referring to Indra Sawhney v. Union of India, it also recognized the value of certainty, consistency, and continuity, but held that compelling reasons may justify departure. Because the statutory provisions were clear and the proceedings predated the Full Bench decision, the principle did not assist the respondents.

predicates.land_ceiling_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning a land-ceiling determination.
predicates.earlier_interpretation_relied_on: A party relies on an earlier judicial interpretation of the governing law.

issues.definition: In a land-ceiling appeal, reliance on an earlier interpretation does not prevent departure from it when the governing text is clear and the proceedings began before that interpretation.
